_comment: VARIABLES: yes|no|partial|death|unknown. Any other will result in a yellow word

Spain.note: Some autonomous communities in Spain offer non-binary gender markers for registration purposes (within their autonomic competences).

France.note: The applicant must demonstrate their claim for legal gender recognition. Minors can not change their legal gender marker. The placement of individuals in prisons is dependant on the legal gender marker.

Egypt.note: While there is no explicit law that criminalizes being transgender, there has been reports of transgender indivualds being criminalized by using broad anti-prostitution and public order laws.

Hungary.note: Gender affirming care is heavily restricted by law. Marriage is restricted to heterosexual couples. Since legal gender change was banned in 2020, only people who transitioned prior to that are allowed to marry as their affirmed gender.

Canada.note: Access to gender affirming care may vary depending on the region.

Israel.note: Changing the legal gender marker and gender affirming care for minors are available, though restricted and subject to rigorous regulations.

China.note: For any type of legal registry to be made, the individual must go through an exhaustive procedure. This includes a diagnosis and having undergone HRT and gender-affirming surgeries, as well as other conditions, such as having no children. Prisons are same-sex, and marriages are exclusively heterosexual. Both of these are based on your legal gender, therefore, it is possible for a trans individual to access such if they complete the legal process.

Russia.note: Transgender individuals may be criminalized under the country's LGBT propaganda laws.

Saudi Arabia.note: Sharia law is broadly applied to criminalize any type of gender nonconformity and make it be punishable by death in some cases.

India.note: Changing the legal gender marker requires gender reassignment surgery except for the non-binary marker. Gender affirming care is accessible, however, there is no structured public health support for it. Some regions have separate hijra/third gender prison facilities. Marriages are exclusive to the opposite sex (listed in the legal gender marker).

Mongolia.note: Gender affirming care access is subjected to heavy bureaucracy.

Germany.note: Minors may get access to gender affirming care with court involvement for citizens under the age of 14.

Italy.note: Legal gender marker change is available through a court order. There is not a strict policy for prisons, every case is revised individually.

Poland.note: Legal gender marker change is available through a court order.

United Kingdom.note: A Gender Recognition Certificate is needed to change a legal gender mark. Gender affirming care through public healthcare is known to have extremely long waitlists. In 2024, hormone blockers for minors were severely restricted.

Kazakhstan.note: Changing legal indicators or gaining access to gender affirming care comes with exhaustive examination including HRT, sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation and exhaustive psychological evaluation.

Netherlands.note: An X legal gender marker can be obtained, but it must be requested through a court order.

Austria.note: Changing the legal gender indicator requires a diagnosis and having undergone HRT. Minors may access HRT, tho it's use is heavily restricted.

Czechia.note: Changing the legal gender indicator requires a diagnosis, and the necessity of having undergone HRT is unclear. HRT and gender affirming surgeries require an evaluation. Marriages must be heterosexual, basing the gender from the legal marker.

Slovakia.note: HRT requires a diagnosis. Surgery is limited.

Slovenia.note: Changing the legal gender indicator is possible, though conditions are unclear. HRT and gender affirming surgeries require an evaluation. Prison placement does not follow a structured procedure.

Switzerland.note: HRT on minors requires evaluation. Prison placement is subjective.

Armenia.note: While not officially classified as a mental illness, heavy stigma and uncertainty still remains. While a legal gender mark change may be possible, there are no stablished legal procedures, and the requirements are uncertain. HRT is heavily regulated. Marriage would be possible in case the legal gender mark has been changed, however, it must be a heterosexual marriage.

Azerbaijan.note: While not officially classified as a mental illness, heavy stigma and uncertainty still remains. HRT and surgery, although technically possible, transgender care is not recognized by the legislation, and are therefore nearly impossible to access in practice.

Belarus.note: Changing one's legal gender mark requires a diagnosis and monotoring for a long period, as well as a forced divorce. Other conditions are unclear, such as the requirement to have no children. The procedure is not available for children. HRT and gender affirming care are heavily restricted. Marriage must be exclusively heterosexual.

Georgia.note: Gender affirming surgery may be available through private clinics.

Moldova.note: A legal gender mark change is only nominally possible. Accessing HRT requires a diagnosis. While technically legal, gender affirming surgeries require a structured framework to be possible in practice.

Ukraine.note: Changing a legal gender mark requires a diagnosis and having undergone HRT, as well as not being available to minors. HRT requires a prescription, and gender affirming surgery requires a psychological evaluation. Marriage must be heterosexual according to legal gender marks.

Denmark.note: HRT and gender affirming surgery are restricted.

Estonia.note: Changing the legal gender indicator, HRT and gender affirming surgery all require a diagnosis. While there is no established policy for placing transgender individuals in prisons, each case may be reviewed individually.

Finland.note: HRT and gender affirming surgery both require a diagnosis.

Latvia.note: Changing one's name is possible if said person has undergone a change of sex. While changing the legal gender marker is possible, the lack of an established procedure makes the conditions unclear. HRT requires a diagnosis, and gender affirming surgeries are limited, and bottom surgeries are typically not performed in-country. Transgender people may get married if the marriage is heterosexual. For same sex marriages, individuals must draw upon a civil union instead.

Lithuania.note: Changing one's name requires permission from the Ministry of Justice and a medical certificate. While changing the legal gender marker is possible, the lack of an established procedure makes the conditions unclear. HRT requires a diagnosis. Transgender people may get married if the marriage is heterosexual. For same sex marriages, individuals must draw upon a civil union instead.

Sweden.note: Changing the legal gender indicator requires an expert testimony, and is available to people above the age of 16. HRT and gender affirming surgery both require a gender dysphoria diagnosis. Prison cases are evaluated case by case.

Albania.note: HRT requires a gender dysphoria diagnosis.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.note: While technically possible by law, a change of name has never been reported. Changing the legal gender indicator requires both a diagnosis and gender reassignment surgery. Prison placement is tied to legal documents. Marriage is exclusively heterosexual.

Bulgaria.note: Changing one's name is nominally possible, but important circumstances that cause ridicule or disgrace, as stated in the Civil Registration Act, must be stated. Therefore, gender may be considered as one. HRT is available through private healthcare.

Croatia.note: Changing the legal gender indicator requires a diagnosis. HRT is partially covered publicly, but is gatekept. Prison placement is based on legal documents. Transgender people can marry as long as it is under a heterosexual marriage.

Cyprus.note: The procedure to change one's legal gender marker is unclear. HRT and gender affirming surgeries are gatekept and require a diagnosis. Prison placements are determined by the legal gender indicator. However, due to the lack of a clear process to change such, it is highly unlikely to be performed. Marriage and joint adoption are reserved to opposite sex couples, though civil unions and adopting as a single parent are alternative options.

Greece.note: HRT and gender affirming surgery are gatekept.

Kosovo.note: HRT is technically legal, but heavily gatekept and practically unavailable. Adoption is only possible as a single parent.

Montenegro.note: Changing the legal gender mark requires having fully transitioned, including having undergone through HRT and gender reassignment surgeries. HRT and surgeries are both gatekept, and although surgeries may be funded by the state, they are performed abroad. Prison placement is determined by the legal gender indicator of the individual, so it is technically possible to be placed on a preferred prison. Marriage is also based in the legal gender indicator, and it is exclusively heterosexual, though same sex couples may go for a civil union. Adoption is reserved for married heterosexual couples. While adopting as a single parent may be possible, the local laws and culture make it virtually impossible.

North Macedonia.note: Although nominally possible, there is no established procedure to change one's legal gender indicator. HRT is heavily gatekept. Marriage would technically be possible if the individual has their legal gender indicator changed and if their marriage is heterosexual. However, the procedure to changing one's legal gender mark is unclear. Adoption is possible as a single parent or as a married couple.

Romania.note: Changing the legal gender indicator requires a diagnosis as well as having undergone HRT, gender reassignment surgery and forced sterilisation. While surgery is not illegal, the country lacks the infrastructure to perform them. Marriage is based on legal gender marker, and is restricted to heterosexual couples. Adoption is only possible either as a single parent or as a opposite-sex married couple.

Serbia.note: A name change is possible as a part of a gender mark change. To change the legal gender mark, individuals must have a diagnosis, undergo HRT and forced sterilisation and be forcefully divorced. HRT and gender affirming surgery are both strictly gatekept. Prison placement is based on the legal gender indicator. Marriage can be possible as long as it is heterosexual. Adoption is possible if the individual is married, and although single parent adoption is technically legal, an openly trans applicant is highly likely to face prejudice and rejection from local social work centers.

Northern Cyprus.note: Changing one's name requires what is known as a justifiable reason. Legal gender may be changed after gender reassignment surgery. HRT is heavily gatekept, and gender reassignment surgery is virtually impossible with the country's infrastructure. Marriage is possible if the legal gender marker is changed and if the marriage is heterosexual. Adoption is available through marriage or as a single parent.

Turkey.note: A legal gender mark change may be available after having undergone gender reassignment surgery. Some other conditions, like HRT, are unclear. HRT is strictly gatekept. Gender affirming surgery, although heavily available, is restricted to citizens. Trans individuals may marry after changing their legal gender mark and as long as the marriage is heterosexual. Adoption must be done through marriage, since despite single parent adoption is possible on paper, Turkey's child welfare authorities are deeply conservative, and are likely to discriminate against trans individuals.

Ireland.note: HRT and gender affirming surgery still rely on a gatekept model. While surgery is not available locally, it is still funded abroad. HRT for minors, is technically possible, however, gender affirming care for minors in ireland is currently in a state of crisis, where infrastructure has been practically non-existent. Prison placements are evaluated case by case.

Luxembourg.note: While surgery is easily available through medical recommendation, it is rarely performed locally, and rather funded abroad.

Australia.note: The hability to change the legal gender indicator may vary depending on the region. An X marker may be available for Australians that provide a birth certificate reflecting an undeterminate sex. Surgery is heavily gatekept and mostly privatized. Minors may get access to HRT, but under very strict circumstances. Prison placements depend on the state, however, most of the time they rely on a case by case basis.

New Zealand.note: Surgery is heavily gatekept and long waitlists are reported. HRT for minors requires consent from the minor, their guardians and a specialized pediatric medical team.

Fiji.note: Although Fiji prohibits discrimination against gender expression, it has got no established procedure to change one's legal gender indicator.

New Caledonia.note: New Caledonia applies the french law. Gender affirming surgery is not available locally, although it is funded abroad.

Papua New Guinea.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, the country's deeply conservative roots and other laws criminalizing same-sex sexual activity may suggest targeting of transgender individuals.

Solomon Islands.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, the country's deeply conservative roots and other laws criminalizing same-sex sexual activity may suggest targeting of transgender individuals. The Solomon Islands have no standing army.

Algeria.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, the country's deeply conservative roots and other laws criminalizing same-sex sexual activity may suggest targeting of transgender individuals.

Libya.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, state actors and armed groups regurarly use broadly written morality laws to prosecute transgender individuals.

Morocco.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, the Moroccan Penal Code may criminalize the trans community, for example, article 483, which criminalizes public indecency, is frequently used to target transgender individuals..

Sudan.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, the Sudanese Penal Code heavily criminalizes the trans community.

Tunisia.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, the Tunisian Penal Code heavily criminalizes the trans community. HRT and surgery is available through specific private channels.

Benin.note: There is no official access for HRT, however, no explicit law criminalizes it. Even so, due to heavy social stigma, transgender individuals are often refused care.

Burkina Faso.note: Although there is no explicit laws against the transgender community, authorities and courts may arrest transgender individuals under broad terms.

Gambia.note: Cross-dressing, as defined in Gambia's Penal Code, can lead to up to 5 years in prison or a heavy fine.

Ghana.note: Any identity outside the male-female binary carries a prison sentence of up to 3 years.

Guinea.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, Guinea's Penal Code heavily criminalizes the trans community.

Ivory Coast.note: Information surounding legal name or gender marker changes is unclear. HRT is not explicitly illegal, but there is no official access. However, it is reported that community-led networks exist.

Liberia.note: Although there is no explicit laws against transgender individuals, the legal environment is heavily weaponized against the trans community.

Mali.note: Approving, encouraging, promoting, or facilitating any act of unsexual nature, as defined in the law, can lead up to 7 years in prison and heavy fines.
